Multivariate GOF test for smooth or random-effect covariates

Source: R/gof.R
gof_multivariate.Rd

Multivariate cumulative-residual test of Boschi & Wit (2025), Section 3.4, for the functional form of one covariate. The covariate's effect is expanded in q = k_basis - 1 event-minus-control columns \(h_i\) of a thin-plate spline basis (mgcv::s()), and the model with these columns and the other covariates linear is refitted without penalty. It contains the linear effect, so it is correct under the null. With its fitted probabilities \(\pi_i\), design rows \(x_i\), inverse information \(V = (X^\top W X)^{-1}\), \(W = \mathrm{diag}\{\pi_i(1-\pi_i)\}\), and score \(\hat U = \sum_i (1-\pi_i) x_i = 0\), the process is $$W(u) = M^{-1/2} \hat J^{-1/2} \Bigl\{\sum_{i \le uM} (1-\pi_i) h_i - A(u) V \hat U\Bigr\},\qquad A(u) = \sum_{i \le uM} \pi_i (1-\pi_i) h_i x_i^\top,$$ with \(\hat J = M^{-1}\sum_i (1-\pi_i)^2 h_i h_i^\top\), and the statistic is \(T_\psi = \sup_u \lVert W(u)\rVert^2\). The second term is zero at the estimate and is written for the replicates, in which it carries the effect of estimating the coefficients. The p-value is the share of n_sim multiplier replicates $$W^*(u) = M^{-1/2} \hat J^{-1/2} \Bigl\{\sum_{i \le uM} g_i (1-\pi_i) h_i - A(u) V \sum_i g_i (1-\pi_i) x_i\Bigr\},\qquad g_i \sim N(0, 1),$$ with \(\sup_u \lVert W^*(u)\rVert^2 \ge T_\psi\) (Lin, Wei & Ying 1993, as in gof_rem()).

Usage

gof_multivariate(
  event_log,
  model,
  covariate,
  k_basis = 5,
  n_sim = 1000,
  scope = "all",
  mode = "one",
  half_life = NULL,
  seed = NULL,
  n_samples = 1
)

Arguments

event_log

Dyadic event log.

model

Named character vector of <stat> = "linear" mapping (for the rest of the model); the test target is covariate with a flexible smooth basis of dimension k_basis - 1.

covariate

Name of the covariate to test under a smooth effect.

k_basis

Spline-basis dimension for covariate (passed as k to mgcv::s(); the resulting design matrix has k_basis - 1 columns under thin-plate identifiability constraints).

n_sim

Number of multiplier-bootstrap replicates for the p-value (default 1000).

scope, mode, half_life, seed

See compare_models().

n_samples

Number of control samples (default 1). With n_samples > 1 the test is run on n_samples case-control samples, drawn with seeds seed, seed + 1, ..., seed + n_samples - 1 (or independently from the current random stream when seed is NULL), and the p-values are combined with the Cauchy combination; see Several control samples.

Value

List with statistic (\(T_\psi\)), p_value, W (n x q matrix), u, covariate and n_sim. With n_samples > 1, p_value is the Cauchy-combined p-value, p_values holds the per-sample p-values and n_samples their number; the other fields are those of the first sample (seed seed). With n_samples = 1 the result is the single-sample result, without p_values or n_samples.

Details

The limit of \(W\) is a Gaussian process with covariance set by how the information \(A(u)\) accumulates over the event sequence. It is a standard \(q\)-dimensional Brownian bridge only when \(A(u)\) grows in proportion to \(u\) in every direction, which fails for the spline columns of a statistic that grows over the sequence (a count): the columns for large values receive their information late. The multiplier replicates have the covariance of the limit whatever the growth of \(A(u)\).

Several control samples

The test is computed on one case-control sample, so its p-value depends on which controls were drawn. With n_samples \(= S > 1\) the p-values \(p_1, \dots, p_S\) of the same test on \(S\) control samples are combined as $$T = \frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^S \tan\{\pi(1/2 - p_s)\}, \qquad p = \frac{1}{2} - \frac{\arctan T}{\pi}$$ (Liu & Xie 2020), the rule gof_global() uses across covariates. The samples share the events, so the \(p_s\) are dependent. The Cauchy combination is valid under arbitrary dependence among the \(p_s\): when each \(p_s\) is uniform under the null, the tail of \(T\) is asymptotically standard Cauchy whatever their dependence (Liu & Xie 2020, Theorem 1), so \(p\) controls the size at small levels; with identical samples it returns their common p-value. Each \(p_s\) is clamped to \([10^{-15}, 1 - 10^{-15}]\) so that the tangent stays finite. The Monte Carlo p-values of gof_multivariate() and gof_auxiliary() are first floored at \(1/(n_{sim} + 1)\) (p_values keeps the unfloored values). Since \(T\) is at most \(\max_s \tan\{\pi(1/2 - p_s)\}\), the combined p-value is then at least \(1/(n_{sim} + 1)\): a combined p-value equal to that bound means \(p < 1/n_{sim}\) in every sample, and a smaller p-value needs a larger n_sim. The Kolmogorov p-values of gof_univariate() and gof_global() are analytic and are not floored.

References

Boschi M, Wit EC (2025). Goodness of fit in relational event models. Statistics and Computing 36(4).

Lin DY, Wei LJ, Ying Z (1993). Checking the Cox model with cumulative sums of martingale-based residuals. Biometrika 80(3), 557–572. doi:10.1093/biomet/80.3.557 .

Liu Y, Xie J (2020). Cauchy combination test: a powerful test with analytic p-value calculation under arbitrary dependency structures. Journal of the American Statistical Association 115(529), 393–402. doi:10.1080/01621459.2018.1554485 .

Examples

if (requireNamespace("mgcv", quietly = TRUE)) {
  data(simulated_events)
  gof_multivariate(simulated_events,
    model = c(reciprocity_count  = "linear",
              transitivity_count = "linear"),
    covariate = "reciprocity_count", n_sim = 200, seed = 1)[c("statistic", "p_value")]
}
#> $statistic
#> [1] 1.514275
#> 
#> $p_value
#> [1] 0.435
#>
